title: Where European finance would feel an AI shock first
summary: A disappointment in AI earnings would initially reach euro area finance chiefly through losses on shares held by investment funds. A disruption at a technology supplier could reach banks and funds even if technology shares held their value. The ECB authors distinguish owning a company, lending to its customers and relying on its services. They find more evidence of common providers and growing portfolio exposure than of AI already causing market-wide forced selling. Greater use of external debt to finance infrastructure could change who bears losses (Charts A.4–A.7).

Among EU enterprises employing at least ten people, about 20% reported using an AI technology in 2025, up around 6.5 percentage points in a year. The definition covers established machine learning as well as newer tools. Chart A.1’s US sector data use a different population and question, limiting international comparisons. Among surveyed euro area banks, the share using generative AI rose from 46% to 86% between 2024 and 2025, while the share still developing it fell from 38% to 10%. About half used it in legal services or IT operations. Including applications under development raises that share to around four fifths. Credit scoring and risk management were much less advanced. A separate international survey of 61 financial institutions found autonomous agents mostly in planning or pilots (Charts A.2–A.3).

Asset managers may lower costs or process information faster, but the fixed costs of systems and oversight could also favour larger firms. Chart A.4 compares active funds that disclose using machine learning with matched peers. In the wider sample with use information, machine-learning funds account for around 15% of roughly $10 trillion in assets. They attracted stronger net inflows between January 2023 and September 2026 and show higher turnover and slightly higher three-year returns after fund-level costs. In a distinct test of equity funds’ daily returns over roughly one year, machine-learning funds were also more likely than matched peers to be in their own lower tail when another fund in their group was already there. A joint test at three tail thresholds gives p = 0.049. Common factor exposures could generate this pattern without identical strategies or forced sales. The study does not observe a fire sale attributable to AI.

Operating risk depends on substitutability. In 2025, AWS, Microsoft and Google accounted for an estimated 82% of the broad European cloud market. Together with OpenAI they accounted for an estimated 90% of EU generative AI services. Those are technology market shares. Bank supervisory returns separately identify the providers institutions name. Two contracts can still depend on the same cloud region or model. The October 2025 AWS outage generated reports in more than 60 countries, chiefly from consumer-facing services. Financial firms supplied relatively few reports. Shared suppliers can afford substantial resilience investment, but simultaneous recovery is a different test from the reliability of each firm’s own systems (Chart A.5).

The authors also score the business descriptions of around 4.5 million companies using a model trained on assessments of a stratified sample of 100,000. One dimension captures ways AI could improve products or work. The other captures threats to prices, demand or the role of the firm. Relative to sample averages, 20% are classified as mainly facing gains, 19% as facing both high gains and threats, and 60% as low on both. Fewer than 0.5% mainly face threats. A firm can have a valuable new tool and still lose margin to rivals. These scores measure potential exposure and cannot establish realised productivity or default probabilities (Chart A.6).

Matching those scores to euro area lending and securities data shows larger exposures in non-bank equity portfolios than in bank loans. When firms cannot be matched directly but their sector is known, exposures are allocated using the distribution of scored firms in that sector. Some counterparties remain unclassified. A separate exercise for 168 AI supply-chain companies and their subsidiaries puts their debt at roughly 0.7% of investment funds’ total debt holdings in the first quarter of 2025 and 1.2% in the second quarter of 2026. Exposure also became more concentrated among major technology firms. Debt and commitments secured on future revenue can spread the cost of an earnings disappointment to creditors. The authors favour tracking this financing alongside tested operational fallback arrangements, governance of sensitive uses and more detailed supervisory information (Chart A.7 and Section 5).

questions.question: Where are losses moving from shareholders to creditors?
questions.detail: Follow debt issuance, claims on future revenues and refinancing schedules for the 168 supply-chain firms and their subsidiaries. Compare the change in investment funds' absolute holdings with their portfolio share, then trace which claims bank lenders ultimately retain. This would distinguish rising leverage at borrowers from rising concentration in holders' portfolios.

questions.question: Can several institutions actually recover a critical service at the same time?
questions.detail: For each important workflow, trace the application through the model supplier and cloud region to the recovery service. Compare the promised fallback with evidence from exercises involving multiple institutions. Two contracts with different suppliers protect against a different set of failures from two demonstrably independent recovery paths.

questions.question: Does excess co-loss survive conventional explanations for common equity risk?
questions.detail: Re-estimate the fund-pair comparison after matching sector and factor exposures, leverage, liquidity and fund size, then split the sample by redemptions. Persistence during high outflows would make overlapping forced sales a more credible transmission mechanism. Similarity confined to shared technology-stock exposure would point to a different monitoring priority.

questions.question: Which companies in the high-opportunity, high-threat group are adapting successfully?
questions.detail: Compare the model's business-description scores with subsequent evidence on adoption, pricing power, margins and debt service. Repeat the portfolio calculation for directly matched issuers alone before adding sector-imputed holdings. The change would show how much the financial exposure estimate depends on broad industry assignments rather than the characteristics of individual borrowers.
